When authors incorporate esoteric concepts, such as the Kabbalah, into their narratives, it can be seen as a form of storytelling that taps into the collective unconscious, as proposed by Carl Jung. This means that the author is drawing upon universal symbols, archetypes, and themes that are shared across cultures and time, rather than simply using them as a gimmick or a way to appear intelligent.

  By incorporating esoteric concepts, authors can create a sense of depth and complexity in their stories, making them more relatable and resonant with readers. It's as if the author is speaking a secret language that only a select few can understand, creating a sense of exclusivity and mystique around the narrative.

  The idea that some authors "intuitively tapped into an archetypal structure" suggests that they have a deep understanding of the human psyche and the collective unconscious, and are able to tap into these universal themes and symbols to create a narrative that speaks to readers on a deeper level.

  This can be seen in the work of authors such as Neil Gaiman, who often incorporates elements of mythology and folklore into his stories, or in the case of Evangelion, the anime series that draws heavily from Jewish mysticism and the Kabbalah. By incorporating these esoteric concepts, authors can create a sense of authenticity and depth in their stories, and can tap into the collective unconscious to create a narrative that resonates with readers.

  However, it's worth noting that not all authors who incorporate esoteric concepts are doing so in a way that is intentional or meaningful. Some may simply be using these concepts as a way to appear intelligent or to add depth to their stories, without truly understanding the underlying symbolism or themes.

  Ultimately, the use of esoteric concepts in storytelling is a complex and multifaceted topic, and can be interpreted in many different ways. Whether or not an author is "tapping into an archetypal structure" is a matter of interpretation, and can depend on the reader's own experiences and perspectives.
